title: Half of India's Coal Plants Critically Low as Record Supplies Chase Surging Demand
excerpt: Ninety-six of 191 plants held less than three days of fuel on October 19. The government says a record 2.6 million tonnes a day is now reaching plants and supply will normalise soon.
body:
• Half of India's 191 coal-fired power plants — 96 plants as of October 19, up from 60 in mid-September — are running on critically low stocks, defined as less than three days of fuel, Central Electricity Authority data show.
  • Total coal stocks at power stations have fallen about 5 percent since the start of October, even as the coal ministry says supplies have been ramped up.
  • The government says it is now delivering a record 2.6 million tonnes of coal a day to power plants and expects supply to normalise soon.
  • For households and factories: peak demand is running 45 to 50 gigawatts above last year, Gujarat has asked factories to curb evening electricity use, and the strain is expected to ease only as temperatures fall and deliveries rebuild stocks.

Half of India's coal-fired power plants are operating with critically low fuel stocks as electricity demand surges in hotter-than-usual weather linked to El Niño, government data reported by Reuters showed. The number of plants with critically low stocks — enough fuel for less than three days of generation — rose to 96 of 191 plants as of October 19, from 60 plants in mid-September, according to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). Total coal stocks at power stations have fallen by about 5 percent since the beginning of October.

Why demand outran supply

Daily peak electricity demand this year has been running about 45 to 50 gigawatts higher than a year earlier. Weaker monsoon rains reduced hydroelectric output and pushed more load onto thermal plants. In September, the gap between demand and supply widened to 560 million kilowatt-hours, the highest since August 2023, even as coal plants raised output. Coal-fired generation rose 13.3 percent in September from a year earlier, while hydropower generation fell 20 percent. India now gets nearly 55 percent of its generation from non-fossil sources, but a lack of batteries to store that clean energy leaves the system dependent on coal during high-demand periods, Reuters reported, in coverage also carried by The Hindu BusinessLine.

The government's response

On Thursday, a senior power ministry official said coal supply to power plants is expected to normalise soon, and that India is supplying a record 2.6 million tonnes of coal to power plants every day, Reuters reported. Supply has been increased to plants including top generator NTPC after scattered rains in mining areas disrupted deliveries. The federal power ministry has allocated additional power to Gujarat, India's top industrial state, and the official said there is no power or coal shortage in the state — a day after Reuters reported that Gujarat had asked factories to curb electricity use during evening hours to avoid shortages. Gujarat state authorities declined to comment on that report.

The coal ministry had already pushed back on shortage warnings earlier in the month. In a statement on October 9, it said supplies to power plants in October were averaging about 9 percent higher than in September and roughly 36 percent above the September low, with rail loading above 465 rakes a day, according to Nation Press. The daily drawdown of stocks had more than halved, from 0.243 million tonnes a day in September to 0.116 million tonnes a day in October, though officials said active stock rebuilding had yet to begin. The ministry also clarified that the 'critical stock' tag is an early-warning threshold, not a sign that a plant has run out of coal or faces imminent shutdown.

What is next

The official case rests on weather and logistics: cooler temperatures should trim demand, and sustained rail loading in the 465 to 475 rakes-a-day range should let deliveries exceed consumption so inventories can rebuild ahead of festive-season and winter demand. The risk is arithmetic. Stocks start that period about 5 percent lower than at the start of October and at roughly half the fleet flagged critical. Until deliveries run ahead of burn for a sustained stretch, any fresh disruption — rain in the mining belts, a rail bottleneck, another heat spike — lands on a system with less than three days of buffer at 96 plants.
